'''Niklas Höhne''' (born October 1970) is a German scientist in the field of national and international climate policy and mitigation of [[greenhouse gas emissions]]. He is founder of the [[NewClimate Institute]] in Cologne, Germany, and professor at [[Wageningen University]].

== Career ==
Höhne attended [[RWTH Aachen University]] with a one-year scholarship at [[INSA Lyon]] and received his Diplom degree in physics in 1997. From 1998 to 2001 he worked as a staff member at the [[UNFCCC]] secretariat. In 2001, he joined Ecofys,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.consultancy.eu/firms/ecofys|title=Ecofys &#124; Consultancy Europe|website=www.consultancy.eu}}</ref> a leading [[climate and energy]] consultancy. In 2005, he received his PhD from the Department of Science, Technology, and Society, [[University of Utrecht]], The Netherlands, for the dissertation on "What is next after the [[Kyoto Protocol]] – Assessment of options for international climate policy post 2012″.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Höhne |first1=Niklas |title=What is next after the Kyoto Protocol? Assessment of options for international climate policy post 2012 |date=2012 |publisher=Techne Press |location=Amsterdam |isbn=978-90-8594-005-0 |url=http://www.technepress.nl/publications.php?id=13}}</ref>
In 2009, he became Director of Energy and Climate Policy at Ecofys. Together with colleagues he founded<ref>{{cite web|url=https://newclimate.org/newclimate-experts/niklas-hoehne/|title=Prof. Dr. Niklas Höhne|website=NewClimate Institute}}</ref> in 2014 the NewClimate Institute, a non-profit research organization for climate policy. In 2017, he was appointed Special Professor<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wur.nl/de/Personen/Niklas-dr.-NE-Niklas-Hoehne.htm|title=dr. NE (Niklas) Hoehne|date=19 September 2012|website=WUR}}</ref> "Mitigation of Greenhouse Gas Emissions" at [[Wageningen University]].

== Research ==
Already in his Diplom thesis "Photothermal deflection spectroscopy as a method to characterize solar cells based on [[amorphous silicon]]"<ref>{{cite book |last1=Höhne |first1=Niklas |title=Photothermal deflection spectroscopy as a method to characterize solar cells based on amorphous silicon |date=1997 |publisher=Diplomarbeit, RWTH Aachen}}</ref> Höhne was devoted to the promotion of [[renewable energy]]. As programme officer at the [[UNFCCC]] secretariat from 1998 on he supported the negotiations on reporting under the [[Kyoto Protocol]], projections of [[greenhouse gas emissions]], fluorinated greenhouse gases and [[Environmental impact of transport|emissions from international transport]]. Höhne led studies related to the international climate change negotiations and national [[Climate policy|climate policies]].

Höhne contributes to reports of the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) since 2003. He is author of the chapter on climate policies and international cooperation in the [[Fourth Assessment Report|Fourth]] and [[Fifth Assessment Report]] and contributing author for the [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report|Sixth Assessment Report]] of the [[IPCC]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ipcc_wg3_ar5_chapter13.pdf|title=13 International Cooperation: Agreements & Instruments – IPCC}}</ref> The IPCC with its authors received the [[Nobel Peace Prize in 2007]].
He is also lead author of all [[UNEP]] [[Emissions Gap report]]s since 2010. He created the [[Climate Action Tracker]] in 2009 that tracks commitments and actions of countries on climate change.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://climateactiontracker.org/press/climate-action-benchmarks-identifying-paris-consistent-pathways-countries-sectors-and-businesses/|title=Climate Action Benchmarks : Identifying Paris-consistent pathways for countries, sectors and businesses|website=climateactiontracker.org}}</ref>

His work with the Climate Action Tracker, the UNEP emissions gap reports and in publications in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rogelj |first1=J |last2=den Elzen |first2=M |last3=Höhne |first3=N |last4=Fransen |first4=T |last5=Fekete |first5=H |last6=Winkler |first6=H |title=Paris Agreement climate proposals need a boost to keep warming well below 2°C |journal=Nature |date=2016 |volume=534 |issue=7609 |pages=631–639 |doi=10.1038/nature18307 |pmid=27357792|bibcode=2016Natur.534..631R |s2cid=205249514 |url=http://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/13307/1/nature18307_proof1.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rogelj |first1=J |last2=Nabel |first2=J |last3=Chen |first3=C |last4=Hare |first4=W |last5=Markmann |first5=K |last6=Meinshausen |first6=M |last7=Schaeffer |first7=M |last8=Macey |first8=K |last9=Höhne |first9=N |title=Copenhagen Accord pledges are paltry |journal=Nature |date=2010 |volume=464 |issue=7292 |pages=1126–1128 |doi=10.1038/4641126a|pmid=20414291 |bibcode=2010Natur.464.1126R |s2cid=4359678 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Höhne |first1=Niklas |last2=den Elzen |first2=Michel |last3=Rogelj |first3=Joeri |last4=Metz |first4=Bert |last5=Fransen |first5=Taryn |last6=Kuramochi |first6=Takeshi |last7=Olhoff |first7=Anne |last8=Alcamo |first8=Joseph |last9=Winkler |first9=Harald |last10=Fu |first10=Sha |last11=Schaeffer |first11=Michiel |last12=Schaeffer |first12=Roberto |last13=Peters |first13=Glen P. |last14=Maxwell |first14=Simon |last15=Dubash |first15=Navroz K. |date=2020-03-04 |title=Emissions: world has four times the work or one-third of the time |journal=Nature |volume=579 |issue=7797 |pages=25–28 |doi=10.1038/d41586-020-00571-x |pmid=32132686 |bibcode=2020Natur.579...25H |s2cid=212408092 |issn=0028-0836|doi-access=free }}</ref> significantly contributed to the understanding that all national [[climate target]]s taken together are not yet compatible with the long-term temperature goal of the [[Paris Agreement]].

Höhne, [[Farhana Yamin]] and Erik Haites were the first to propose in 2013 a global goal for a future international climate agreement to phase out greenhouse gas emissions entirely.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Haites |first1=Erik |last2=Yamin |first2=Farhana |last3=Höhne |first3=Niklas |date=October 2013 |title=Possible Elements of a 2015 Legal Agreement on Climate Change |url=https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/possible-elements-of-a-2015-legal-agreement-on-climate-change/ |access-date=2022-08-28 |website=[[Wageningen University]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haites |first1=Erik |last2=Yamin |first2=Farhana |last3=Höhne |first3=Niklas |title=Possible Elements of a 2015 Agreement to Address Climate Change |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24323952 |journal=Carbon & Climate Law Review |year=2014 |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=3–12 |jstor=24323952 }}</ref>
This idea was eventually included in the Paris Agreement adopted in 2015 as "to achieve a balance between anthropogenic emissions by sources and removals by sinks of greenhouse gases in the second half of this century", the so-called net zero emissions goal. Accordingly, many countries set themselves national net zero emissions goals. Höhne and colleagues were the first to find that the full implementation of this wave of national net zero goals would bring the long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement within reach.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2021 |title=Wave of net zero emission targets opens window to meeting the Paris Agreement |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-021-01142-2 |journal=[[Nature Climate Change]] |volume=11 |pages=820–822|doi=10.1038/s41558-021-01142-2 |bibcode=2021NatCC..11..820H |last1=Höhne |first1=Niklas |last2=Gidden |first2=Matthew J. |last3=Den Elzen |first3=Michel |last4=Hans |first4=Frederic |last5=Fyson |first5=Claire |last6=Geiges |first6=Andreas |last7=Jeffery |first7=M. Louise |last8=Gonzales-Zuñiga |first8=Sofia |last9=Mooldijk |first9=Silke |last10=Hare |first10=William |last11=Rogelj |first11=Joeri |issue=10 |s2cid=237539819 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

He and colleagues broke down the challenge of net-zero global greenhouse gas emissions into actionable sectoral benchmarks. For example, in 2016, they argued that this would mean the end of sales of cars with [[internal combustion engine]]s by 2035.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-11-16 |title=The ten most important short-term steps to limit warming to 1.5°C |url=https://climateactiontracker.org/publications/the-ten-most-important-short-term-steps-to-limit-warming-to-15c/ |access-date=2022-08-28 |website=Climate Action Tracker}}</ref> In 2021, the IEA ([[International Energy Agency]]) picked up this goal.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 2021 |title=Net Zero by 2050 A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector |url=https://www.iea.org/reports/net-zero-by-2050 |access-date=2022-08-27 |website=IEA}} fig. page 20</ref> Finally in 2022, the EU adopted this date in their regulation on {{CO2}} emissions from cars and vans.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-08-27 |title=CO₂ emission performance standards for cars and vans |url=https://ec.europa.eu/clima/eu-action/european-green-deal/delivering-european-green-deal/co2-emission-performance-standards-cars-and-vans_en |access-date=2022-08-27 |website=European Commission}}</ref>

His PhD thesis work of 2005 on sharing the effort of reducing greenhouse gas emissions between countries contains the statement that [[developed countries]] would need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25% to 40% in 2020 compared to 1990 and 80% to 95% by 2050 to be compatible with limiting global temperature increase to 2&nbsp;°C.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gupta |first1=S. |last2=Tirpak |first2=D. |last3=Burger |first3=N. |last4=Gupta |first4=J.|author4-link=Joyeeta Gupta |last5=Höhne |first5=N. |last6=Boncheva |first6=A.I. |last7=Kanoan |first7=G.M. |last8=Kolstad |first8=C. |last9=Kruger |first9=J.A. |last10=Michaelowa |first10=A. |last11=Murase |first11=S. |last12=Pershing |first12=J. |last13=Saijo |first13=T. |last14=Sari |first14=A. |title=Policies, Instruments and Co-operative Arrangements, Climate Change 2007: Mitigation. Contribution of Working Group III to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |date=2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK, and New York, NY |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/ar4-wg3-chapter13-2.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=den Elzen |first1=M.G.J. |last2=Höhne |first2=N. |title=Reductions of greenhouse gas emissions in Annex I and non-Annex I countries for meeting concentration stabilisation targets. An editorial comment. |journal=Climatic Change |date=2008 |volume=91 |issue=3–4 |pages=249–274 |doi=10.1007/s10584-008-9484-z|doi-access=free |bibcode=2008ClCh...91..249D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=den Elzen |first1=M.G.J. |last2=Höhne |first2=N. |title=Sharing the reduction effort to limit global warming to 2°C. |journal=Climate Policy |date=2010 |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=247–260 |doi=10.3763/cpol.2009.0678a|bibcode=2010CliPo..10..247D |s2cid=152964846 }}</ref>
These values were picked up in the [[IPCC Fourth Assessment Report]] and became the internationally agreed standard for the required reductions by developed countries at that time and inspired many national greenhouse gas emission reduction targets, e.g. Norway, Japan, German, EU, Korea, Mexico, US.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-03-08 |title=Communication From The Commission To The European Parliament, The Council, The European Economic And Social Committee And The Committee Of The Regions |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52011DC0112&from=EN |access-date=2022-08-27 |website=European Commission}}</ref>
